title: Edgecase attention anecdotes — Ryan H. (2026-09)
content:
Quick brain-dump after reading a handful of papers + two conference talks. This is explicitly informal: half sketches, half hypotheses, lots of open questions. Goal is to surface small, local experiments we can run on Redwood's serving runtime in the next 2–3 sprints.

1) Overfitting of attention to early context ("attention degeneracy") — what's the phenomenon?
- Anecdote: long customer convo where a single trigger token at t=10 keeps getting high attention even after topic drift to t=250. Model keeps repeating the same framing.
- Hypothesis: repeated prefix patterns + caching cause KV similarity to amplify, producing a local attractor in attention space.
- Quick probe idea: synth dataset of repeated prefixes (A B B B ... then new topic C) and measure attention mass on prefix tokens as sequence grows. Use our runtime to vary KV shard placement and cache eviction schedule.
- Metric: fraction of total attention weight on tokens < 32 positions from start, normalized by token frequency.

2) KV-cache eviction policies and tail latency tradeoffs
- Current: simple LRU-ish eviction per incoming request. Works for bursty workloads but might preserve stale attractors.
- Thought: implement a "recency+novelty" score: score = alpha * recency + beta * 1/(1 + cluster-similarity-to-current). If cached KV entries are very similar to incoming prefix, keep; if similar but old, penalize.
- Experiment: run A/B on small dedicated pool. Route synthetic workload with topic shifts. Measure perplexity drift, top-1 token churn, tokens served per second, and p95 latency.

3) Micro-caching for tail queries (cheap wins)
- Many tail queries are short, repeated (support replies), or templated. Micro-cache first 8 tokens per route for 5s TTL.
- Danger: staleness for personalized responses. Add a quick check: if request includes user_id, bypass micro-cache by default.
- Implementation notes: integrate into request preprocessor in serving-runtime; TTL table sharded per model route.

4) Attention collapse under low-bit quantization
- Paper summary: some quantization schemes compress attention heads unevenly; heads that carry rare-but-important signals collapse, causing subtle accuracy regressions on long-context tasks.
- Quick test: quantize model to 4-bit using our optimize profile A and run one-shot QA over documents with rare anchor tokens. Compare logits distribution across heads before/after.
- Possible mitigation: per-head calibration step or higher-precision KV for selected heads.

5) Small experiment matrix for next sprint (concrete)
- E1: Synthetic attractor probe. 50 prefixes x varying repeat counts (1, 5, 20). Measure attention mass shift. (low effort)
- E2: Micro-cache rollout on a Canary route for 48 hours. Collect error rates and serving cost delta. (medium effort)
- E3: KV eviction policy patch (recency+novelty) behind flag. Replay 3 weeks of anonymized production trace and compute quality/cost difference. (higher effort)
- E4: Head-wise quantization calibration on a small 7B model. Evaluate on rare-anchor QA set. (medium-high)

6) Open questions / dumb ideas to validate
- Could we use a lightweight "attention novelty" score at run-time to detect attractor events and trigger a soft reset (flush tail of KV) for that request? Risk: harms coherence for genuinely long-range dependencies.
- Is there signal in user-agent / client pattern to decide micro-cache TTL per route? e.g., web UI vs API client.
- Can we cheaply estimate per-head importance by running short drop-head ablations on small batches in the background?

7) Notes to self for implementation:
- Build probe harness as a small Docker job that can run on the dev cluster. Use existing replay utilities (gh:redwood-inference/trace-replay).
- Keep experiments reproducible: commit seed files to experiment folder and tag with model, quant profile, runtime commit.
- Add telemetry hooks for any KV eviction change: old_keys_evicted, similarity_score_hist, cause_tag.

References / quick reads I skimmed while writing:
- "Transformers are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Generation with Linear Attention" (for intuition on attention caching). arXiv:2102.06171
- Blog: "When Attention Goes Wrong" — short taxonomy of failure modes (not rigorous, but good examples).
- Talk notes from InferenceSummit 2026: session "Long-Context Attractors"

Actionable next steps (1–3):
- [ ] Implement E1 probe harness and run across two small models (7B and 13B) by next Wed.
- [ ] Draft RFC for micro-cache canary (include opt-out via user_id header). Ping Maya for infra review.
- [ ] Add telemetry fields to KV eviction path RFC; start replay for E3 once eviction patch exists.

Random aside / heuristic: when in doubt, prefer conservative cache eviction for traffic with high user churn; prefer keeping cache for templated system messages.

Questions I want to discuss with Maya/SRE:
- Is there a perf budget to run periodic ablation jobs on the dedicated cluster? (I think yes but need confirmation)
- Any constraints on adding third-field telemetry histograms to production traces?

Footer: these are scribbles — will clean into an RFC if E1 shows measurable attractor effect.

-- Ryan
summary: Personal scratchpad describing attention attractor phenomenon, KV-cache eviction ideas, micro-caching proposal, quantization-head risks, and a 4-experiment plan for short-term validation. Includes references and a three-item immediate action list.
